paper_title: Disen-Forcing: Disentangling Semantic Anchoring from Motion for Autoregressive Video Diffusion

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Autoregressive video diffusion models (AR-VDMs) enable real-time, long-horizon video generation but degrade rapidly once the inference horizon outruns the training horizon, due to compounding exposure bias. To stabilize long rollouts, recent methods heuristically adopt frame sink, keeping initial frames as a persistent model context, inspired by attention sinks in LLMs. We revisit this design and find that the mechanism by which initial frames stabilize long-range consistency in AR-VDMs is not an LLM-style attention sink; instead, long-range consistency is anchored through a sparse subset of attention heads, while the majority of heads predominantly capture local temporal dynamics. This observation reveals an over-conditioning pathology in existing frame-sink strategies: by universally exposing every head to the pinned initial-frame context, the model becomes prone to collapsing motion toward the low-dynamic modes of the teacher during model distillation. We propose Disen-Forcing, a distillation-time plug-in for AR-VDMs that disentangles and reinforces this head specialization through disentangled context routing and motion-disentangling regularization. On long-horizon video generation benchmarks, Disen-Forcing simultaneously improves long-range consistency and motion dynamics of base AR-VDMs, a trade-off that sink-based methods fail to balance.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Recent advances in video diffusion models (VDMs) have enabled photorealistic and temporally coherent video synthesis [6, 7, 17, 24]. However, most VDMs employ bidirectional temporal attention, generating all frames in parallel without respecting temporal order, which limits their use in real-time or interactive applications. Autoregressive video diffusion models (AR-VDMs) [4, 19, 52] have emerged as promising alternative, applying per-frame diffusion denoising in causal order. This hybrid paradigm retains diffusions high-fidelity sample quality while enabling streaming generation, key capability for real-time interactive world models [1, 27, 30, 33]. fundamental challenge in AR-VDMs is exposure bias [37, 53] (Section 3.1): as each newly generated frame is fed back as future conditioning, small generation errors accumulate over rollout steps, progressively degrading visual quality and semantic consistency. This issue is exacerbated by traininginference mismatch in horizon and context quality: training typically exposes the model to limited-length rollouts and relatively clean context, whereas inference often requires much longer extrapolation under increasingly error-corrupted self-generated history. Self-Forcing [19] mitigates exposure bias by training on self-generated rollouts, but drift still emerges when the inference horizon exceeds the training horizon. To solve this, the de facto stabilization heuristic is frame sink [29, 47, 49] (Section 3.1), which pins the initial frames in the KV cache throughout model rollout, inspired by attention sinks in streaming LLMs [45]a design that implicitly treats initial frames as universal attention attractor, i.e., shared global reference for all heads. While it improves long-range semantic consistency, it often suppresses temporal dynamics, yielding conservative motion (Section 3.3). In this work, by analyzing the temporal attention patterns of AR-VDMs (Section 3.2), we find that initial frames do not act as universal attention attractor as in LLM-style attention sinks; instead, they anchor semantic consistency through sparse, stable subset of anchor heads. This reveals an over-conditioning in the existing frame sink strategy, which universally exposes every head to the initial-frame context. Under the mode-seeking distillation objective [51], this universalization causes the student to collapse motion toward the low-variance, near-static modes of the teacher (Section 3.3). Building on these observations, we propose Disen-Forcing, distillation-time plug-in for AR-VDMs that disentangles and reinforces the head specialization through two complementary components: disentangled context routing (Section 4.1) replaces the universal sink during DMD with per-head-type contexts: only anchor heads retain access to the initial frames, while the rest are restricted to the local sliding window, eliminating the over-conditioning; motion-disentangling regularization (Section 4.2) imposes an invariance constraint preventing anchor heads from leaking global semantics into motion, directly suppressing the remaining semantic-to-motion leakage after routing. Our contributions are: Diagnosis: revealing that initial frames in AR-VDMs do not act as universal attention sinks; instead, semantic anchoring is concentrated in sparse, stable subset of anchor heads, exposing universal frame-sink conditioning as cause of motion collapse under DMD. Method: proposing Disen-Forcing, distillation-time plug-in that reinforces this head specialization via disentangled context routing and motion-disentangling regularization. Results: demonstrating on long-horizon video benchmarks that Disen-Forcing improves both motion dynamics and long-range consistency over base AR-VDMs, resolving tradeoff that existing sink-based methods cannot balance.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: AR-VDMs. Video diffusion models (VDMs) [6, 7, 11, 14, 16, 24, 40, 41, 43, 48, 54] generate high-fidelity content with coherent temporal dynamics. Autoregression (AR), established in language modeling [3] and token-based video generation [18], also enables incremental video synthesis. Rolling-denoising methods [22, 23, 29, 34, 39, 46] progressively denoise and advance temporal window, whereas FramePack [53] compresses historical context for next-frame-section prediction. Diffusion Forcing [4] trains with independent per-frame noise levels; History Guidance [38] extends this formulation to non-causal transformers. SkyReels-V2 [5] and MAGI-1 [36] use ordered frameor chunk-wise noise schedules for long-video generation. Within this diffusion-AR hybrid paradigm, CausVid [52] attains few-step causal inference through Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) [50, 51], while Self-Forcing [19] retains the DMD objective and narrows the traintest gap by feeding the 2 models own rollout as context during training. Causal-Forcing [56] further improves initialization by distilling ODE trajectories from an autoregressive teacher. Despite training on self-generated context, temporal drift still emerges when inference exceeds the training horizon. Attention Sinks in LLMs. The attention sink phenomenon [45] in AR LLMsdisproportionate attention to the first few input tokens regardless of semantic contentemerges with large-scale next-token prediction training [13]. These tokens act as no-op attention score absorbers [2]; pinning them as persistent context stabilizes streaming inference over arbitrarily long sequences [45]. Sink-based AR-VDMs. Inspired by LLM attention sinks, the frame sink heuristic [8, 9, 25, 26, 29, 47, 49] has been widely adopted in AR-VDMs to alleviate long-horizon drift by pinning initial frames as persistent context. We show that, in AR-VDMs, sink-like attention to initial frames is not ubiquitous across heads but concentrated in sparse subset of heads (Section 3.2); universally exposing every head to the pinned context drives motion collapse under mode-seeking distillation (Section 3.3).

sections.title: 3 Rethinking the Frame Sink Strategy in AR-VDMs
sections.content: In this section, we begin by revisiting AR-VDMs, their exposure bias, and the frame sink heuristic (Section 3.1). Then we show that initial frames are not universal attention sink but clean reference exploited by sparse subset of attention heads for global consistency (Section 3.2). Finally, we identify motion collapse as the consequence of universalizing this role across all heads (Section 3.3). 3.1 Preliminaries: AR-VDMs and Anti-Drift with Frame Sink Exposure Bias in AR-VDMs. An AR-VDM is hybrid model that combines the strengths of AR models in temporal modeling and diffusion models in continuous distribution modeling. Specifically, it uses the AR chain-rule decomposition to factorize the joint distribution of video sequence x1:N = (x1, x2, . . . , xN ) into product of conditionals1: p(x1:N ) = (cid:81)N i=1 p(xi x<i). Each conditional p(xi x<i) is modeled by diffusion process that denoises Gaussian noise into video frame conditioned on previously generated frames. These conditionals can be learned with denoising [4] or flow-matching [28] objectives. In Teacher Forcing, the conditional at noise level x<i tj is formed as p(xi 0 ), with clean ground-truth history frames. In Diffusion Forcing [4], the tj conditional is instead p(xi ), where history frames are corrupted with independent noise levels. tj Both formulations introduce traintest gap termed exposure bias [37]: the context exposed to the model is ground-truth during training but self-generated at inference. x<i t0 Causal Distillation. As an alternative to the above methods, CausVid [52] shifts toward causal distillation. This is typically achieved through Distribution Matching Distillation [51] (DMD). Rather than training with per-frame denoising objective on ground-truth videos, causal student model Gθ, initialized by regression on the bidirectional teachers ODE trajectories [19, 52], is distilled to directly build noisedata mapping, using the holistic fidelity of its generated videos under the teachers distribution as its learning signal. Concretely, DMD minimizes the reverse KL divergence between the student distribution qθ,t and the teacher distribution pt at diffusion timestep [44, 51], with gradient θLDMD = Et (cid:2)θ KL(qθ,t pt)(cid:3). (1) Training with the distribution-matching loss enables few-step sampling without paired teacher trajectories. Self-Forcing [19] further mitigates the traintest gap by conditioning the model on self-rollout frames during distillation. Self-Forcing implements history conditioning through causal self-attention with KV cache [19, 52]. Since the context x<i grows unboundedly with AR steps, Self-Forcing adopts sliding window attention (Fig. 5 (a)), which is also referred to as rolling KV cache, approximating p(xi x<i) by qθ(xi xiw:i1), retaining only the most recent frames. Although self-rollout training alleviates exposure bias, severe error compounding still occurs once inference extrapolates beyond the training horizon. Anti-Drift with Frame Sink. Recent works [29, 47] empirically identify that retaining initial frames as frame sink [47] in the sliding window attention, i.e., qθ(xi x1, xiw:i1)a strategy analogous to the attention sinks in LLMs [45], is effective at maintaining long-range semantic 1Each xi may represent single frame or chunk of frames; we use frame and chunk interchangeably for brevity. 3 consistency during frame-length extrapolation. While this heuristic mitigates appearance drift from error accumulation, the role of initial frames in preventing drift remains unclear. In LLMs, the attention sink refers to phenomenon where most heads assign disproportionate attention mass to the first few tokens, which act as no-ops absorbing probability mass in the absence of relevant context (Section 2). natural question arises: do initial frame tokens serve the same role in AR-VDMs? (a) Per-head attention across AR-VDMs (b) Representative Self-Forcing heads over rollout steps Figure 2: Temporal attention patterns across models and heads. (a) Per-head attention to the initial and current frames across AR-VDMs, averaged over 50 MovieGenBench [32] prompts and denoising timesteps. Most heads attend predominantly to the current frame, while sparse subset concentrates attention on the initial frame. (b) Attention distributions of representative Self-Forcing heads across seven rollout steps, at ODE initialization (left) and after DMD (right). Working Heads exhibit local temporal patterns, whereas Anchor Heads attend persistently to the initial frame. 3.2 Uncovering the Anti-Drift Role of Initial Frames Initial Frames Are Not Universal Attention Sink. To uncover the mechanism of initial frames in anti-drift, we examine per-head attention scores across layers and AR steps. We observe that the attention landscape in AR-VDMs is fundamentally different from that in LLMs. Specifically, we measure the average attention allocated to the initial frames versus the current frame for every head, averaged over 50 MovieGenBench [32] prompts and all diffusion timesteps. As shown in Fig. 2a, the vast majority of heads attend predominantly to the current framenot the initial frames. In other words, the current frame, rather than the initial ones, plays role similar to the universal attention sink in LLMs. We conjecture that the difference between the LLM and AR-VDM sink patterns stems from two factors. Data: in language, adjacent tokens are discrete and typically less redundant than adjacent video frames, which often share substantial visual content. Objective: In LLMs, the prediction target is future token outside the input; under causal masking, initial tokens are uniquely visible to every query and naturally absorb the resulting attention mass as sinks [45]. AR-VDMs, in contrast, denoise the current frame from its own noisy latent at each AR step: the denoising target is located at the current-frame position itself. Together with the strong spatio-temporal redundancy of video tokens, this encourages attention to concentrate on the current frame. Figure 3: Critical Role of Anchor Heads in Semantic Consistency. Masking the top 20% Anchor Heads leads to sharp drop in subject/background consistency and clear rise in imaging-quality drift (left), together with visible appearance drift even within the 5-second training horizon (right). Masking the same number of Working Heads at random yields metrics on par with the unmasked baseline and no observable drift. Initial Frames Sustain Consistency through Sparse Heads. To discover what truly enables initial frames in anti-drift, we visualize per-head attention distributions throughout the AR rollout (Fig. 2b; representative head-wise attention grids in Fig. A2). While most heads exhibit local temporal pattern, sparse subset, concentrated in specific layers (e.g., layers 18 and 2224 of the 30-layer Wan2.1 [40] backbone), exhibits persistent attention spikes toward the initial frame. Based on this observation, we categorize attention heads into two types: Working HeadsThe vast majority of heads, which attend predominantly to the local sliding window context; and Anchor HeadsA sparse minority of heads that attend strongly to the initial frame across AR steps. universal attention sink would absorb the majority of the attention mass across heads; the observed sparsity of Anchor Heads suggests different mechanism. From the attention pattern, we hypothesize that these sparse Anchor Heads exploit the initial frames as clean reference with minimal cumulative error, stabilizing long-range consistency. We test this via head-masking experiment  (Fig. 3)  : during inference within the 5-second Self-Forcing training horizon, we mask the top-20% anchor heads (by average initial-frame attention score). This causes visible appearance drift even within the training horizon. In contrast, masking the same number of randomly selected Working Heads produces no observable drift (more samples in Fig. A6). Together, the two head types reveal division of labor: Anchor Heads sustain global semantic consistency by preserving reference to the initial frames, while Working Heads focus on local temporal dynamics, as reflected in their local attention pattern. Figure 4: Anchor-head positions are input invariant. (a) Each row plots single prompts per-head initial-frame attention score. The same vertical stripes are coherent across all 50 rows, meaning the same subset of heads attends strongly to the initial frame regardless of prompt. (b) Each row plots the per-head cross-prompt mean attention score at one of the four diffusion timesteps. The four rows display the same vertical stripes, indicating timestep-invariance as well. Stability of the Head Partition. We find the partition pattern to be stable across inputs and training stages. Fig. 4 shows that largely overlapping subset of heads consistently exhibits elevated initialframe attention across diverse prompts and diffusion timesteps. The partition is also already present in the ODE-initialization model and the anchor-head locations remain stable after distillation (e.g., 5 comparing Self-Forcing and its ODE-initialization in Fig. 2). Notably, similar partition emerges in the bidirectional teacher backbone (Section D), suggesting the structure is rooted in pretraining rather than the AR distillation pipeline. Together, these observations indicate that the anchor/working partition is structural property of the pretrained model rather than an artifact of any particular distillation stage. 3.3 Motion Collapse from Universal Frame Sink The above analysis shows that initial frames stabilize global consistency sparsely through the Anchor Heads. In current sink-based AR-VDMs, however, the initial frames are exposed to every head via the shared KV context [Kinit; Kwin; Kcur], [Vinit; Vwin; Vcur], including the majority of Working Heads that focus on local dynamics. Combined with the mode-seeking DMD objective [50, 51], this universal conditioning offers the student an easy shortcut toward high-fidelity static modes. The initial frames provide clean reference with minimal exposure bias, unlike the sliding window, which accumulates self-rollout error. Static or near-static outputs that closely track this reference, therefore, tend to score higher on consistency than more dynamic outputs (Fig. 6 and Table 1). Such static modes also remain probable under the teacher distribution, since pretraining video datasets usually contain substantial fraction of static scenes. With universal access to Kinit and Vinit, every headincluding the Working Heads normally responsible for local dynamicscan exploit this shortcut, leading the student to over-condition on the initial frames at the cost of motion.

sections.title: 4 The Disen-Forcing Method
sections.content: Building on the above analysis, frame sink rests on universal attention sink premise that does not hold in AR-VDMs and overlooks the observed head specialization. We therefore propose DisenForcing, distillation-time plug-in for AR-VDMs that respects this specialization during distillation. Given an ODE-initialization model (Section 3.1), we first perform one-time identification of anchor heads, then distill with two complementary components: disentangled context routing (Section 4.1) that gives each head type its functional context, and motion-disentangling regularization (Section 4.2) that prevents anchor heads from inducing motion collapse. Figure 5: Disentangled context routing. (a) Sliding window attention loses early frames as the cache rolls forward. (b) Sinked sliding window retains initial frames but routes the same context to all heads. (c) During DMD, our approach routes initial-frame context exclusively to the sparse Anchor Heads while the majority Working Heads attend only to the local sliding window, preserving the natural head specialization. 4.1 Disentangled Context Routing The motion collapse issue reveals an over-conditioning of the frame sink heuristic on initial-frame context. Inspired by the observation of specialized head types in Section 3.2, we propose to assign each head type dedicated context that matches its functional role, shielding Working Heads from the static initial-frame reference and thereby eliminating the over-reliance at its source. sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: Implementation details. We implement Disen-Forcing as distillation-time plug-in on SelfForcing [19] and Causal-Forcing [56]. Both base models are four-step causal AR-VDMs based on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, with 5-second training horizon and an 832480 resolution. We finetune each base model from its own ODE-initialization checkpoint with KV cache size of 9 latent frames3 initial, 3 sliding-window, and 3 current frames. Each AR rollout step denoises chunk of 3 latent frames, and the 5-second training horizon corresponds to 7 such rollout steps. Distillation runs on VidProM [42]. We use batch size of 64, except for Self-Forcing + Disen-Forcing and the ablations, which use 32. The anchor head set is identified using all 1003 MovieGenBench [32] prompts by thresholding at the 80th percentile. Its stability across prompts and sample sizes is evaluated in Figs. 4 and A4. We apply motion-disentangling regularization to layer 26 (S = {26} in Eq. (3)) with weight λreg = 0.002. Layer selection is evaluated in Section E.1. See Section for more details. 7 Figure 6: Qualitative comparison and ablation. Self-Forcing suffers from temporal drift once the inference rollout exceeds the training horizon; Frame Sink avoids temporal drift but yields lowdynamic, conservative motion. Ours (Disen-Forcing) is both drift-free and temporally dynamic. The bottom block isolates the contributions of our two components: context routing and Lreg. Evaluation. We evaluate on 200 MovieGenBench [32] prompts using the indices published by Rolling-Forcing [29]. We generate 30-second and 1-minute videos at 16 fps, covering the long-video horizons also studied in prior work [49]. We use VBench-Long [20, 21] across six dimensions: subject consistency, background consistency, motion smoothness, dynamic degree, aesthetic quality, and imaging quality. We report all six dimensions on 0100 scale and their mean (Total). Following Zhang et al. [53], temporal drift is measured as the mean absolute imaging quality gap between the first and last segments (Q Drift). 5.1 Comparison with Existing Models Baselines. Our primary baselines are the Frame Sink variants of Self-Forcing and Causal-Forcing, each distilled from the same ODE checkpoint as its Disen-Forcing counterpart under matched compute (identical KV cache size and iterations). This isolates the contribution of Disen-Forcing beyond the frame sink alone. We further compare against three sliding-window AR-VDMs (CausVid [52], SelfForcing [19], Causal-Forcing [56]), three sink-based methods (LongLive [47], Rolling-Forcing [29], Deep-Forcing [49]), and the diffusion-forcing model SkyReels-V2 [5]. In our evaluation, all baselines use 4 denoising steps except Rolling-Forcing (5) and SkyReels-V2 (30, undistilled). Results. Table 1 reveals two failure modes of existing models. The base models lose early-frame context as the cache rolls forward and accumulate severe drift, while their Frame Sink variants recover consistency but suppress motion. Disen-Forcing improves both motion dynamics and long-range consistency over both base models. Finally, we study the regularization-layer selection by comparing individual candidate layers with their joint regularization, and vary the regularization weight λreg to examine its effect on temporal dynamics and consistency. Full per-dimension results and additional ablations are reported in Appendix E. Context Routing. sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: In this work, we revisit the anti-drift role of initial frames in AR-VDMs and find that the implicit assumption underlying existing methodsthat initial frames serve as universal attention sinkdoes not hold. Instead, anti-drift is carried by sparse, stable subset of anchor heads, separate from majority working heads that attend locally. Building upon this observation, we propose Disen-Forcing, distillation-time plug-in with two components: disentangled context routing restricts initial-frame access to anchor heads, and motion-disentangling regularization enforces motion construction to remain invariant under initial-frame conditioning. Extensive experiments show that Disen-Forcing improves both motion dynamics and long-range consistency over the base AR-VDMs.

sections.content: A.1 Training Configurations Training setup. We use AdamW with (β1, β2) = (0.0, 0.999) for both the generator and the critic, with learning rates 2106 and 4107 respectively. The critic and generator are updated in 5:1 ratio (5 critic updates per generator update). We apply an exponential moving average (EMA) on the generator weights with decay 0.99, starting at effective step 200. Models are sharded across 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs using FSDP with hybrid-full sharding and size-based wrapping. We enable gradient checkpointing during training. full training run of 600 effective steps takes approximately 14 hours. RoPE configuration. We store keys without RoPE in the KV cache and apply RoPE when using the cached keys to compute attention. Initial frames are positioned immediately before the local sliding window in temporal position space, following Infinite-Forcing [8] and Rolling-Forcing [29]. A.2 More Details on Motion-Disentangling Regularization Regularization computation. Fig. A1 summarizes the computation. The motion-disentangling regularization compares cross-frame attention maps from two passes: the standard forward (with disentangled routing) and the counterfactual pass (with Anchor Heads KV replaced). We use forward KL divergence KL(sg( ˆA) A), with the counterfactual proxy ˆA as the stop-gradient target for the standard proxy A. For each query frame i, the cross-frame attention map is computed against the immediately preceding frame i1 (adjacent matching); its effect is evaluated in Table A4. Without adjacent matching, all query frames instead match the oldest frame in the sliding window. VAE re-encoding for the counterfactual pass. Wan-VAE [40] uses causal temporal convolutions with feature caching: the initial chunk has no preceding feature context, unlike later chunks. This creates distribution difference between initialand later-chunk latents. Since Anchor Heads are trained to attend to these initial-chunk tokens, directly using sliding-window tokens as the anchor-side keys/values in the counterfactual pass places Anchor Heads out-of-distribution. To eliminate this token distribution gap, before each counterfactual pass, we VAE-decode the sliding-window context to pixels and re-encode it back to latents without conditioning on prior context, mirroring the encoding pathway of the initial chunk. Table A4 evaluates the effect of this re-encoding. Attention-map computation. The model forward retains FlashAttention [10]. sections.title: C Additional Qualitative Results
sections.content: C.1 Anchor Head Masking Experiment Masking protocol. To probe the functional role of Anchor Heads during inference, we run the trained Self-Forcing checkpoint with three masking conditions: (1) no mask (the unmodified rollout), (2) random mask (zero out the keys/values of randomly selected 20% of heads in each layer, excluding identified anchor heads), and (3) anchor mask (zero out the keys/values of the heads identified as anchors in (Section 4.1)). To isolate the role of anchor heads in the long-range anti-drift mechanism rather than in within-chunk denoising, masking is applied only to the earliestresident KV frame in the sliding window, and only for AR rollout steps beyond the first chunk. All other settings, including the prompt and random seed, are identical across conditions. As shown in Fig. A6, randomly masking working heads produces videos with similar visual quality to the no-mask baseline, while anchor masking induces visible appearance driftcolor shifts, identity inconsistency, and scene degradationeven within the 5-second training horizon. This pattern complements the quantitative VBench-Long results in Fig. 3 and confirms that the anti-drift role is specifically carried by the sparse anchor-head subset rather than by attention heads in general. 18 Figure A5: VideoScore preference rates on 30s generations. Percentages compare the three methods within each base model and evaluation dimension. Figure A6: Qualitative anchor-head masking comparison across prompts. Each row shows one prompt rendered under three masking conditions: no mask (baseline, left block), mask random heads (control, middle block, blue), and mask anchor heads (treatment, right block, red). Each block displays three frames spanning the 5-second clip. brief prompt description is shown below each row. Random masking preserves visual fidelity; anchor masking produces visible identity, color, and scene drift, confirming that long-range anti-drift is carried specifically by the anchor-head subset. A7 and A8 cover the 1-minute setting, and Figs. A9 and A10 cover the 30-second setting. Across prompts, sliding-window methods drift visibly past the training horizon, sink-based methods preserve appearance but suppress motion, and +Disen-Forcing maintains both consistency and motion dynamics. Discussion: When Does Head-Type Separation Emerge? We investigate when the anchor/working head-type partition arises by measuring the same temporal attention distribution in pretrained bidirectional Wan backbones, prior to any causal AR adaptation or distillation. The partition is structural property of the pretrained backbone. As shown in Fig. A11, the bidirectional Wan2.1-1.3B, Wan2.1-14B, and Wan2.2-TI2V-5B base models [40] all exhibit the same characteristic pattern: the vast majority of heads attend predominantly to the current frame, while Figure A7: 1-minute qualitative comparison. Figure A8: 1-minute qualitative comparison. sparse, stable subset shows concentrated attention to the initial frame. This is consistent with the pattern observed in the distilled AR-VDM variants of Fig. 2a. The anchor/working partition is therefore not induced by causal AR training or DMD distillation it is inherited from the pretrained backbone and further reinforced during distillation. The pattern scales to larger models. The same structural separation is observed in the 14B parameter variant of Wan2.1 (Fig. A11, middle): sparse subset of heads shows elevated initial-frame attention at both the earliest layers (02) and the deepest layers (28, 32, 3638), while the majority attend predominantly to the current frame. The pattern further transfers to Wan2.2-TI2V-5B (Fig. A11, 20 Figure A9: 30-second qualitative comparison. right) despite substantial architectural changes (per-token time modulation, unified cross-attention, 41616 high-compression VAE). This suggests that the head-type partition is robust property across both model scales and Wan generations, and that Disen-Forcings disentangled routing and regularization can in principle be applied to more powerful AR-VDMs in future work. The partition extends beyond Wan. We additionally analyze HunyuanVideo-13B [24] and CogVideoX-5B [48]. sections.title: F Discussions
sections.content: Limitations and Future Work Disen-Forcing operates as distillation-time plug-in and inherits the pretraining biases of the base model; it does not address artifacts originating from the bidirectional teacher itself. Its performance is further limited by the ODE initialization. The motion-disentangling regularization also requires counterfactual forward pass during training, introducing small per-step cost on the generator side (Table A1). Several directions remain open. First, extending Disen-Forcing to the Wan2.1-14B and Wan2.2-TI2V-5B backbones, where the same anchor/working partition emerges (Fig. A11), and examining whether the routing principle generalizes to image-conditioned long-horizon generation. Second, while our instantiation builds on DMD distillation, extending the framework to other distillation objectives such as SiD-style losses [55] or GAN-based objectives [12] is natural next step. Finally, it would be worthwhile to investigate whether disentangling semantic anchoring from motion can also benefit the ODE initialization stage itself. Broader Impacts Disen-Forcing improves the visual quality and long-range consistency of longhorizon video generation, which has applications in education, accessibility, and creative tools, but shares standard dual-use considerations of generative video models (e.g., misuse for synthetic media). The method is fine-tuning plug-in on existing public AR-VDMs and does not in itself introduce new generative capability beyond those baselines.
